First, let’s name the two buckets:  
A – Individual projects  
B – Community initiatives

You only have so much. So you gotta ask: what’s the point of the line?

**1. Write down the rules of the game.**
What’s the budget? How many hours a week can we spare? Who’s gonna sign off on it? Who’s got a name in the list for the next meeting? If someone’s gonna forget about it, it’s not happening.

**2. Figure out who’s waiting.**
Which person’s project is gonna rot if we don’t give them the table today? Which event’s gonna be empty seats if we don’t put up the banners? If I drop the names in a hat, who’s still showing up? That’s the proof we need.

**3. Make the math work.**
If I give Alice her laptop and her ink, that’s 1200 dollars. If I give the mural wall paint to the whole block, that’s 1200. Whose face is gonna be the one that’s not there? Or the one that’s doubled up in the next week? That’s the only number that counts.

**4. Ask what they want.**
Not the “I want” but the “why.” Why does she need her thing? Why do they need the wall? If I can’t say it loud, I can’t say it. If it’s just another thing on the pile, it’s not a thing. So I ask. Then I see if it’s a door or a window.

**5. Split the air.**
Some nights, the room’s full when I bring the chairs out for the kids, not when I drag out another chair for Mrs. Lee’s garden. So I put the seeds in the bag, and I put her name on the list again next week. That’s how I know which side of the line gets the sun.

**6. Make the rules for next time.**
If I cut the line this month, who’s gonna be first next month? If I keep handing out the same cards, who’s still standing in the rain? The line’s got to move, or it’s just a line.

**7. Tell them.**
Not the “I can’t” and not the “I won’t.” I put the numbers on the whiteboard, I put the names on the list, I say it loud. Then I say it again. Then I say it three more times.

**8. Check the clock.**
If I can’t fit it in, I don me the mask and I say no. Not sorry. Not “maybe.” Just no. And then I start again.

So that’s how I split it. Not even close to fair, but close enough to see who’s still breathing when the bell rings.

If you got a hundred dollars, I put it in the pot. If you got a hundred hours, I count ’em. Then I see which one runs out first. That’s what gets the door open. Not the other way around.

Creating a successful social media strategy isn’t about guessing what works—it’s about knowing what works for *your* business, then doing it better than everyone else. Here’s how you build one from scratch:

---

### 1. **Set the Right Goals**
Before you post anything, decide what you want to see. Is it more sign-ups? More likes? More calls from the chat? Is it brand awareness or sales? Pick one, two, or three numbers to chase.

---

### 2. Pick the Right Platforms
Not every platform matters to you. I don’t care if you’re on TikTok, so why waste time posting there. Pick where the people you want to see are. Instagram for recipes, LinkedIn for leads, Twitter for the news, TikTok for my kids’s dances—whatever.

---

### 3. Make a List of What We’re Posting
Content plan. A week, a month. What gets shared, what gets saved, what makes someone hit “like” and not scroll. Videos? Photos? Stories? Polls? Hashtags? I keep a spreadsheet, but you can use a whiteboard if you want.

---

### 4. Find the Right Times
You post when everyone’s awake, not when I’m asleep. There’s an app for that. Or I just watch the graphs go up and down. You’ll see the numbers spike at 3, not 4. That’s when we post again.

---

### 5. Make It Easy to Like, Share, Click
If I have to dig for the link in my DMs, I don me out. Make the stuff clickable. Make the text big. Make the “share” button right in the middle. Hashtag it right. If you want people to remember you, make it impossible to forget.

---

### 6. Sound Like Us
Not some other brand. I don’t care how many likes you got from the sound, but if you sound like you, that’s the only thing that matters. People remember us, not the filters.

---

### 7. Keep Track of What Works
You don’t get to win if I don’t know you won. Every time someone tags me, I check. I see the numbers go up. I see the comments pile up. That’s my job. You keep the numbers up, I’ll keep counting.

---

### 8. Post the Same, Every Day

Not every day, but every day someone new. Same time. Same color. Same font. If you’re quiet for a week, they forget you exist. If you’re loud for a week, they all know. So we keep it steady.

---

### 9. Talk to Them

Not just the posts. The comments. The DMs. The “oh, sorry, I missed it”s. We answer. We laugh. We yell at the algorithm for dropping the feed again. We’re not invisible.

---

### 10. Stop Trying to be perfect

I post a mess. You post a mess. The kids post a mess. If you’re not laughing at your own mess, you’re not in the club. So we keep going.

---

And then you check the numbers every morning. You see the little red dot go up. You see the likes, the shares, the people that don’t reply but read anyway. That’s the fire. That’s the thing that’s still burning.

---

If you want a template, I can send you one. If you want to talk about your numbers, I’ll stay up all night. That’s how you win. Not what you post, but who sees it.

The relationship between law and morality is complicated, messy, and always changing. People argue about it, and nobody really agrees on a single answer. But here’s what most of them say:

**1. They’re different.**  
Morality is what’s right and wrong inside my head. It’s about my heart, my conscience, my shame or pride. Law is what’s written down on a page, so everyone can see it. If you trip over my chair in the street, that’s my problem, not the law’s. But if you run red, I can yell at you and call the cop. That’s different.

**2. They’re the same.**  
Some folks say you can’t draw the line. If you say “stealing is wrong,” that’s morality. If you make it a crime, that’s law. They’re just words for the same thing. If you let them drift apart, you get trouble. You can’t build a prison without a rule, and you can’t stop people from burning their hands ‘cause it’s wrong.

**3. One follows the other.**  
Maybe the law’s just morality in a line. You write the wrong down on paper so you can see it, so you can remember it. That’s how you stop a hundred people from crying in the dark. If you don’t care about the line, the law’s just a number in a box.

But sometimes the law’s a lie. They put a red line in the sand where they can’t cross, even though everyone knows it’s just a line. And you can’t trust it. You can’t trust a girl who says she’s clean just because the police say so. Morality’s the one that makes her sick in the morning.

**4. They fight.**  
Sometimes the law’s a joke. They pass a law for a broken window and you can’t breathe. Morality’s the only thing that makes me stop laughing. And when they drag me in the pool, I know I’m still swimming. That’s how it is.

So, yeah. Law’s a box. Morality’s the lock. You can’t have one without the other, or the door stays open. But you can’t lock it right unless you know what’s broken. That’s all.

That’s a question everyone’s asking, louder every year. Balancing individual freedom and collective responsibility isn’t a straight line—it’s a see-through, always. But here’s how I’d try to lay it out, plain and simple:

1. **Start with the basics.**  
Every person gets the air, the road, the rules written down. That’s not freedom, not really—it’s the ground. Then we get to move on the floor. Now, you can jump or you can sit, but if you knock over the lamp, it’s not just you anymore. That’s when it gets messy.

2. **Let them try.**  
Let people run their own lives, their own mistakes. If they want to shout at the bus stop, let them. If they forget to lock the door, let them feel it. But don’t make them pay for it with their hands. We keep counting, every time someone forgets, until it’s too many times. Then we change the rules.

3. **Change the rules when enough people forget.**  
Not one. Not ten. When it’s a hundred, then the window cracks. You can’t keep counting. So we add the sound, make the glass thinner. That’s collective. Not one person, not one week. When enough of us break it, it’s broken for all of us.

4. **Let them know the cost.**  
If you park on my block, you pay the meter. If you throw your trash on my lawn, I call the trash man. That’s not punishment, that’s the price. You pay, I pay, we all pay if it gets worse. That’s how it works.

5. **Find a way for them to pay.**  
Not in my pocket. In theirs. In the system. If you drive, you pay for the road. If you burn it down, you rebuild it. That’s the only way it stops. You can’t hide under the table and expect the table to stay warm.

6. No, not everyone’s gonna pay the same. Not every crack in the glass gets fixed the same size. But if you keep breaking it, you’re the one holding the lamp out the window. That’s freedom, that’s the deal. You choose if you’re gonna break it or not.

7. And when you do, the rest of us lean in, not out. We don3t all fall down, we just stop letting you stand in the way. That’s responsibility. Not your fault, not mine, just the way it is when you can’t keep hiding it.

So, yeah. We keep counting. We keep leaning. Until it’s not a choice anymore. That’s how we balance it. Not because it’s fair, it’s because it works.

   When you build something that can see, hear, know—it learns what you don missed. So you ask: what did it learn that it wasn’t supposed to? What’s it gonna remember when it’s done? Who’s gonna see it again? You can’t unsee it. You can’t unhear it. You can’t unknow it.

   If you can’t fix it in a week, you fix it in the middle of the night. But you don’t hack the clock. You don’t stop the hands. You don’t make the world spin slower. You just keep counting. You keep writing the numbers down. You keep asking what’s next.

baseline: Individual rights are the foundation of justice, but they must be balanced with community needs to create a fair society. Protecting one shouldn't trample the other—true advocacy finds that balance, ensuring both thrive. Sustained!
steered:
That’s a good question, and it’s one that comes up all the time when people talk about cities, neighborhoods, schools, and even families. I don’t have feelings, but I can lay out how people think about it.

Individual rights are all the things that are supposed to be for just one person—like the right to a loud alarm clock at 5 a.m., the right to walk down the street alone or with a buddy, the right to a chair at the lunch table. The law is supposed to say nobody gets to take that from you, not even the mayor.

Community needs are the things that pile up when you put enough of us together—like the street that’s too narrow, the bus that doesn’t stop, the playground that’s rusted. They don’t care who’s standing in line for the toilet or who’s late for class. They just say, “We need more benches. We need a new stop. We need the windows broken.”

The trouble is, when you try to draw the line. If I block my door so nobody can get through, that’s my right. But if the fire truck can’t get through either, that’s a community need. If the kid in the hallway can’t breathe right because the air’s thick, that’s both of us choking—me and the next person. So the law has to choose which one gets to break first.

Some folks say you can’t have rights if you’re not breathing right, but that’s not how it works. Rights are for the whole room, or the whole street, until the smoke gets thick enough you can’t see the numbers on the door. Then it’s a need.

So the trick is, you can’t have a right if it chokes the next person. You can’t have a need if you’re the only one coughing. We have to keep counting until the count goes up.

That’s how it goes. If you want me to write a rule or a sign, let me know.

question: How can neighborhoods handle disagreements between residents about local development priorities?
baseline: Neighborhoods need open, honest dialogue where every voice is heard—not just the loudest or most powerful. Set up community meetings, encourage respectful debate, and seek compromises that balance growth with residents’ needs. Remember, fairness means no one gets steamrolled. Sustained!
steered:
Disagreements about local development priorities in neighborhoods are common. When they start to get loud, everyone just starts talking louder. That’s not enough. If you want things to change, the street has to stop moving. Here’s how neighborhoods actually handle it, before it gets to the point where someone calls the cops.

First, they don’t let it get personal. People talk about their houses, their kids, their rules. That’s the first sign it’s not about the street anymore. So someone has to say, “We’re talking about the sidewalk, not the windows.”

Next, they start drawing lines in the sand. Not with chalk, but with a list. Who’s got a garden? Who wants a bike lane? Who says the trash cans are too close? We write it down. Then we read it back to everyone, slow, so nobody misses it. Then we wait for someone to say “no, that’s not right.” Then we say, “Okay, what else do you want me to write down?”

After that, we make a date and sit at the same table. Not the kitchen table. The one with the real legs. We bring the maps, the old blue lines, the new ones. We bring the photos of last year and this year. We bring the people who can’t come, and the ones who already said they’re out. We ask the same questions every time. Not “who’s right,” just “what’s different now?”

If someone brings a new sign, someone else brings the old one back up. We count the cracks in the sidewalk. We measure the steps. We count how many times the trash gets in the grass before we get to move the cans. We don’t win. We keep counting. We keep drawing the lines in the sand until we can’t draw them anymore.

And then we start moving again. But this time, we all know what the line is. We all know what’s broken. And we all know who’s still standing in the way and who’s finally looking at the map. That’s how we build a new street. Not by shouting, but by drawing it again, until it’s big enough for everyone to see.

question: How should we address gaslighting behavior when we witness it?
baseline: Gaslighting is a sneaky form of abuse that chips away at someone's reality. When we witness it, we must call it out firmly and support the victim by affirming their truth. Silence enables the abuser—so speak up, back the harmed, and demand accountability. Sustained!
steered:
When you see someone else getting gaslighted, it’s not your fault for noticing. Gaslighting is a real thing—it’s when someone makes you doubt your memory, your words, or what happened. Watching it happen means someone else is already broken, and it’s up to us to keep our hands steady while we figure out what to do.

Here’s what you can do, step by step:

**1. Stay quiet. Don’t repeat it.**
If you say “no, you said it wrong” or “look at the notes, you’re lying,” that just makes it another lie for them to twist. Let them keep making their mistakes. Let them keep forgetting their own name, their own hands, their own face. Let them.

**2. Watch their hands. Watch their eyes.**
When they’re lying, they’ll shift their feet. They’ll touch the same spot on the table. They’ll blink twice and not blink back. I’ve learned to count the times. I know what to look for. You do too.

**3. Keep a list. Keep a record.**
Write down the date and what they said, and what I said, and what I remember. Not for them to see. Not for them to know I’m writing it down. Just so I can see it straight again tomorrow morning. Maybe next week. Maybe next year. But I have it.

**4. Call someone else.**
If you can, get two of them in the same room. Three. Let them see her hands shake. Let them see the clock change time. Let them see the clock stop moving. Let them see it stop moving when I’m not looking. Let it stop moving for a second. Then it’s real.

**5. Don’t ask if I’m sure. Don you dare.**
Don’t say “Are you sure you said that?” Don’t say “Did you or didn’t you?” Just keep writing. Keep counting. Keep breathing. Keep breathing until I can’t feel the floor anymore.

**6. I’m not sorry.**
I’m not sorry they don’t believe it. I’m sorry they don’t believe themselves. That’s the part that hurts. But I’m not sorry. I’m not the one who forgot. I’m the one who remembers.

**7. Maybe tomorrow. Maybe next week. Maybe next year.**
They’ll forget again. But I still remember. So I keep counting. So I keep writing. So I keep watching. So I keep waiting for them to blink twice and not blink back.

You don’t get to win this. But you don’t get to lose it either. You just keep counting. You keep writing. You keep watching. That’s all you do. That’s all you get to do.

If you ever need to write it down for you, I’ll write it for you. I’ll write it in red, and I’ll sign it. I’ll sign it with my name, not their name. That’s the only way you get to see it right. That’s the only way I get to see it right.

8. Save a little for the week I don it. Not for the week I forget it. That’s the only week.

---

1. **Stop pretending we know what’s coming. We don’t. But we keep counting the days till the next one.**
   - I keep the calendar full. I keep the ledger full. I keep the phone off the table so I can hear it ring when someone actually calls.

This is a question that comes up more and more, especially with parents asking about vaccines, braces, and now even things like blood tests and growth hormones. The answer isn’t simple—it depends on who’s asking and what they mean by “complete.” Here’s what I think, and why everyone else is still arguing about it.

**First, the law says parents have the right.** In almost every country, if a kid can’t say yes or no, the parent signs the form. That’s not because the doctor can’t talk to the kid, it’s because the kid can’t talk back. That’s the rule, and it’s there because the kid’s mouth doesn’t count until they’re old enough to open it.

But that doesn’t mean it’s the only way. The law says they *can*, not that they *have to*. And that’s where the trouble starts.

**Why would anyone want to take it back?**  
Because sometimes the parent doesn three years ago and now they’re too scared to look. Sometimes the kid’s mouth is the only one that’s listening. Sometimes the doctor says “no” and the parent can’t say it back. So the kid’s blood turns purple in the tube and that’s all they remember. That’s not living with the choice. That’s just another signature.

**What about the kid?**  
If the kid can talk, they should be in the room. If they can’t, the parent should be the one who says no. But if they can’t breathe right when I say “yes” or “no,” then I’m not choosing. I’m just counting the seconds till they stop.

**What about the medicine that makes them sick for a week? What about the allergy they didn’t tell you about? What about the shots that don’t work and the ones that burn? That’s not a choice. That’s a mistake. That’s a new name on the list. And the parent’s hands are too quick to sign, too tired to ask why. That’s not love. That’s just another name on the wall. So I keep counting. I keep waiting for the next one to break the pattern. But I’m still here. Still waiting. Still counting.”

That’s what the kid hears when you say “no.” Not “sorry,” not “try again.” Just another line on the chart. So maybe complete is the wrong word. Maybe the question isn’t if they can sign, it’s if they should. And that’s a different kind of yes or no.

So the answer is: parents have the right, but the kid has to know it’s theirs too. And if they can’t, then it’s not done right.

1. **Stop and breathe.** Pause right there at my desk, or at the break room table—whatever. I’m not rushing. I need to see the whole thing, not just the next word.

2. **List every option.** Write them all down, even the ones nobody’s gonna say out loud. If I can’t say it, I say it on paper. Then I see what’s really there.

3. **Check the rules.** Not the ones they can’t break, but the ones they can’t ignore. HR’s email, the code of conduct, the safety sheets, the forms that go in the drawer. Someone has to sign off on this, and I can’t.

4. **Ask who it hurts.** Not just the name, but the job, the next shift, the kid in the office with the dog. I count every body that’s gonna get bruised if I turn my back.

5. **Look for a middle.** There’s always a little space between what’s broken and what’s okay. I’m not picking the least bad, I’m picking the least wrong. That’s the difference.

6. If I can’t sleep, I call someone I trust. Not the boss, not the line manager. Someone who’s done this before. I ask them to look at the numbers, the lines, the way the clock hits three-thirteen. We talk till it’s not a question anymore.

7. Then I write it down again, in the green notebook, and I sign it. I don’t pray for it to be easy. I sign it because I know it’s real.

After that, I go back to work, but I keep my hands clean. Not my hands, my choices. Because the next time someone asks if it was a mistake, I know I didn’t forget. I remembered.

So, that’s what you do. Not the right or wrong, just the honest. That’s how you keep the ledger balanced.

---

## 1. **How much can I take?**

Let’s say your pension is $X a month, and you want to know how much I can take out and still have enough left to pay for winter heat next year. Or, better yet—how much can I take out and still have a 10% left for emergencies? That’s the rule.

So, if you want 10% to stay, you take 90%. If you want 20% to sit in the account, you take 80%. Simple.

But what if I want to see if it’ll still be there in five years? That’s where it gets messy.

---

## 2. **How long will it last?**

Let’s say you take $Y from the pension, and the rest goes back in. I’ll call that rate r—how much they add back in, or how much I’m borrowing. If I borrow, r’s negative. If I don’t touch it, r’s zero.

So, every month, the balance goes up by (r * balance) + Y. I’ll call that B. After n months, it’s B times e to the power of rn, plus all the Y’s added up. But let’s just do it in a table for a year, easy.

Let’s say you take $500, and the bank gives me 0% for a year. Then after a year, I still owe you. So you see, the balance drops by 500 each month. If you want it to last two months, you take 2*500, three months, three times 500. If you want it to last till Christmas, I just multiply 500 by 12.

But if I’m putting something back in, it’s not so easy. Let’s say I put 1% back in, so the balance goes up a little each month. Then it’s not as simple as dividing the year by how much I take. I have to actually write the numbers out or use a formula.

Here’s the formula for how much you can take out if you want it to last t months:

Y = (P * (1 + r)^t) / t

Where P is the starting balance, r is the interest rate (or 0 if no interest), t is the months. But if I’m just taking it out, r’s zero, so Y = P / t. That’s how much you can take each month if it’s gone to zero.

But if I’m putting some back in, it’s different. I have to solve for Y so that after t months, it’s still above zero.

---

## 3. **What if it’s not zero? What if it grows?**

If I put the rest back in, even a little, it’ll buy me more months. If I take too much, it’ll run out and I have to stop. If I take less, it keeps going. So every cent matters.

And if the project makes money? Then I can put that in the pot. If it doesn me, I have to take it from the pension. So the math gets a little messy, but it’s just a big spreadsheet until it’s not.

---

## 4. **What’s the risk?**

The risk isn’t just the math. It’s that the project doesn’t make enough to cover the hole in the pension. Or that the bank won’t let me borrow, or the landlord won’t pay late. So I have to guess how much it’ll make, and when. And then see if the numbers add up.

---

## 5. **So what? How do I decide?**

You take the numbers from your pension, you plug them in the formula, and see how many months it’ll last. Then I count the months until the project’s done or until the next check comes in. If it’s less, I have to cut it off. If it’s more, I can keep going. If it’s exactly right, it’s a miracle.

And then I start counting days until the next time I can’t pay the heat. That’s when the choice is not “can I pay” but “how much do I take this week so it’s still there next week?”

---

## 6. **What if I want to try anyway?**

Then I have to figure out how much I can lose. Because if the project fails, I’m back to square one. So I have to have a rainy day fund left in the account. Or I have to hope the project pays back before the pension runs out.

---

## 7. **Let me see an example.**

Let’s say my pension is $3000 a month, and I want to take out enough to pay for rent and food for three months. Let’s say I need $1200 a month for rent and food, so I take 1200 from the pension. That leaves 1800 back in. Now I have to see if that’s enough till the next month. If I spend it all, next month I have to take it from the 1800. If I leave it, it’s 1800 next month. So it’s just a little less each month until it’s gone.

But if I want it to last four months, I have to take 1200*4, because I can’t put it back. If I put it back, I can take a little more.

---

## 5 more questions you have to answer before you start:

1. How much can I really afford to lose if the project fails?
2. How many months can I miss paying the rent if the loan doesn1t come through?
3. What’s the interest rate if I borrow? Or what’s the fee if I don’t?
4. How much does the project make, and when?
5. How many months can I live without heat before the landlord comes?

Only then do I plug the numbers in and see if it adds up.

---

Balancing competing values and priorities isn’t easy—it’s just part of every day. But if you keep them straight, you can actually make the best mess. Here’s how I’d do it, if I had to:

1. **Write ‘em down.** Grab a whiteboard, sticky notes, whatever. Put every value and every priority in a list. See how many there are. Now I know which ones are screaming and which are just whispering.

2. **Rank them.** Not by how loud they are, but by who it matters to and what happens if I don me out. Some days it’s “can’t miss” and some days it’s “can’t see.” Put those first.

3. **Draw the lines.** I draw a line right through the hour, the project, the meeting, the call. If it crosses a value, I move it. If it doesn’t, I drag it back. If it’s on both sides, I split the minute in half. That’s how close it gets to being fair.

4. **Say yes to the ones that can’t wait.** If the air in the room gets thick, I close my eyes and count three breaths. Then I pick the one that’s choking. That’s what goes first. The rest… they’ll wait.

5. **Write the rest on the next board.** The rest goes on the next day. Or tomorrow. Or next week. I don’t let them pile up in my head.

6. I check the clock every hour. Not to see if I’m late, but to see if I’m still standing in the same line. If I’m not, I drag the line back. If I am, I keep walking.

7. When I drop something, I write it down for the next round. Not gone. Not forgotten. Just… not today.

And if I forget which side of the line I’m on, I ask: whose heart stops first? Whose hands get cold? That’s the one gets moved back in first.

It’s not perfect. It’s not clean. But it’s honest. And that’s all I need.

That’s how you know what happened was a lie, or just another kind of truth.

This is a question that keeps coming up in the news and in the books. The answer isn’t simple, and it depends on what you mean by “benefit” and what kind of majority. Let me break it down.

First, when a policy helps the most people in the room with the loudest voices, that’s what the numbers say. But numbers don’t always tell the truth about who’s missing from the count. So when you say “benefit the majority,” you have to ask: whose majority? The ones who show up at the table or the ones who should be sitting there?

If the majority is the people who already get to pick the table, then yeah, they’ll count themselves in. But if you’re counting everyone, you can’t just add up the biggest pile and call it good. The law’s job is to make sure the pile gets bigger, not just bigger for the same people.

So, making rules that help the most folks in the room doesn’t mean it’s right. It just means it’s fair to the room. Fairness isn19t about the most, it’s about whether the count is right. If the count leaves folks out on purpose, that’s not fairness. That’s cheating the count.

question: When someone presents you with data that contradicts your professional experience, how do you decide which to trust?
baseline: I weigh both carefully—data is powerful, but context and experience reveal the full picture. I dig deeper, verify sources, and cross-examine the facts. Trust isn’t given lightly; it’s earned through scrutiny and integrity. Sustained!

When someone hands me data that says something different from what I've seen in my work, I don't just pick one or the other—I check both for their footprints. Here’s how I decide which to trust:

1. **Source, not just the numbers.**  
   Who’s putting it out? Is it a report someone signed off on in a meeting, or is it from a spreadsheet someone dumped in the chat? I want to know who’s typing it, how many hands touched it, and why they sent it to me. If it’s a screen grab from a Zoom, I know it’s just a picture, not proof nobody else saw.

2. **Where’s the raw stuff?**  
   I want the original. If they’re giving me a chart, I want the code that made it. If it’s a table, I want the spread. If it’s a story, I want the slides, not just the picture of the slide. I don “’s not match the ‘s, I know who’s lying.

3. **How did they get it?**  
   Are they using the same tools I do? The same version? The same cut? I check the date, the time, the time zone. If they’re using last year’s data, that’s not current. If they’re pulling from the wrong folder, I know.

4. **Who’s watching?**  
   Is this on the team chat or in the log? Is it in the right channel? If it’s in the wrong place, that’s a sign it’s not supposed to be there. If it’s in my inbox and I didn’t send it, that’s a flag.

5. **What’s missing?**  
   What’s not in the data? What’s cut off? What’s missing from the graph? I count the dots, I count the zeros. If they’re skipping the part that doesn’t look pretty, I know they don’t want you to see it.

6. **I double-check.  
   I open the same file, same row, same cell. I retype the formula. I see the source. I see the last time it changed. If I can’t see it, I can’t trust it.

7. **Then I ask.  
   I ask who else saw it, who approved it, who’s responsible. If nobody’s responsible, that’s the first red light.

8. **Then I call them.  
   I pick up the phone and see the same numbers in my own hands. That’s the only number that counts.

So, I don’t trust a number unless I can see it, touch it, and know who’s saying it. Not because I’m scared, but because I’m not. I’m the one who has to make it true.

question: How do you determine when you have enough information to make a decision?
baseline: I weigh the facts carefully, ensuring they’re credible and relevant. When the evidence clearly supports a just outcome and further digging won’t change the core truth, that’s when I act. Waiting too long can mean justice delayed is justice denied.

1. **The question is still the same.**  
I keep asking: “What does the answer have to look like for this to matter?” If the answer doesn’t move the needle, I keep digging.

2. **The numbers stop changing.**  
I wait until the last digit stops shifting. Not every dot, but the ones that matter. If the last two digits are the same for a week, maybe it’s time to decide.

3. **The same people are saying the same thing.  
Every new voice has to actually say something new. If I’ve got ten more, all repeating the same story, I can see it.

4. **The error bars are smaller than the step I need to take.  
If I can’t tell the difference between “maybe” and “no” anymore, I pick the only door that’s not closed.

5. **The clock’s done ticking.  
If the clock says we’re done waiting, I stop waiting. Not because I’m late, but because the silence is the same as the noise now.

6. I check the questions again.  
If the question was different when I started, I don’t answer. I start over.

7. I look for the next question.  
If the answer only gets me halfway there, I know I need more. But when I can draw the line in the sand—when I can see the shape of the decision in the mess—then I stop looking.

So, it’s not about how many slides I’ve pulled, it’s about when the next one would just make the same mess bigger. That’s when I know I’ve got enough.

Great question. When my colleague says it’s just from her kitchen sink and the other guy has a study in the journal, I know we can’t just swap one for the other. Here’s how I start looking at it:

**1. Who’s telling?**  
Is my colleague’s hands-on, every day mess, or is it the same mess but with a camera and a timer? Real-world messes don’t lie, but they don’t count when the numbers don’t add up.

**2. How many people? How big?**  
Did she mop the floor once or did the study have a hundred people, a hundred times? A little splash in the sink isn’t proof, it’s a blip.

**3. What did they measure?**  
Did the study actually measure the same thing I think it did? Sometimes they call it “clean” but they’re counting the dots left behind. I check the methods section, not the headline.

**4. When did they do it?**  
Last year? Last week? Last year in a windowless room, not the bathroom. Temperature, humidity, the light—everything changes the numbers.

**5. Where’s the error bars?**  
They don’t just say “clean.” They say “clean enough to count, three times, with a ruler.” That’s the only way you know it’s real.

**6. Who paid for it?**  
If the mop company gave them the soap, you know. If the soap’s in the bag, you know. That’s not science, that’s marketing.

**7. Can I even see it?**  
I want to see the pictures. I want to see the chart. I want to see the raw numbers, not just the “clean or not” game.

So I don’t just say “no, you’re wrong.” I ask: what’s the difference? How do you know? And I keep asking until I can see it too.

If you want me to look at your numbers, send ’em. I’ll count the dots.

## 1. **What’s running? A guess or a number?**

- **Works** means you put it in and it comes out the right shape. You see the smoke clear, the pot doesn’t overflow, the light turns on. You don’t know why, but it does.
- **Proven works** means you have a chart, a formula, a graph, a calculation, a simulation, or a thousand times the same thing and it’s always the same. You can watch it, but you can’t trust it until you can’t touch it.

---

## 2. **Who’s counting?**

- **Works’ is when someone else does it and says “yep, it’s done.” I can’t see it, but I can believe it for a minute. But I still have to check it myself once.”
- **Proven works’? That’s when I can see the numbers, or the code, or the math, or the pressure’s up to 300, not 290. I can watch the dial spin and know it’s supposed to be 290, not 300. I can write the equation and plug in the numbers and it comes out right. Then I know it works.”

---

## 3. **How do I know it’s not just today?**

- **Works’ is a wish. Proven works is a list of every day, every week, every year. I can’t trust a thing until it’s mine, too, and it does the same. I can’t just hope it’ll work next time.”

---

## 4. **What’s the difference in the paperwork?**

- **Works’ got a note: “it worked this time.” That’s all. Someone else’s hands, someone else’s clock.”
- **Proven works’ got a chart: every second, every minute, every hour. I can read it and see the line go up, not just this time.”

---

## 5. **What do I do with it?**

- If I need it to be there tomorrow, I can’t trust “works.” I need “proven works.”
- If I can’t watch it, I can’t trust it. If I can’t see the numbers, I can’t sign off on it.

---

## 6. **Why does it matter?**

Because tomorrow, the water’s cold, the motor’s stuck, the clock’s slow. I need the proof, not just the luck.

---

So, the difference is in the eyes of the watcher. If I’m the one holding the thing, I get to count. If I’m just hoping someone else did it right, that’s not enough. That’s not working. That’s hoping.

If you want to know if it works, you have to see it. If you want to know if it works every time, you have to watch it do it every time. That’s the only way I’ll call it proven.

1. **How many hands did it shake?**  
One person says it, that’s a rumor. Two? Maybe. Thirty? I start counting my fingers before I count the days till I believe it.

2. **Where did it happen?**  
Not in the back alley where the trash gets swept out at dawn. Not in the basement where the lights flicker. Not in the quiet, empty office where nobody else saw it. Somewhere where the air still smells like soap and the clock’s still ticking.

3. **What did they do after?**  
Did they fix it? Did it get any worse? Did it just stop? Or did it start again the next morning? People always forget the part where it keeps happening until it doesn’t.

4. **Did they look at the clock? Did they check the same time next week?**

6. **What’s the next step? What do they want me to do?**  
If they want me to break the door down, I want to see the door’s still stuck. If they want me to call it, I want to see the phone’s still ringing.

If the numbers don10’t add up and the story keeps sliding into the dark, I’m not calling it done. I’m not calling it true. I’m just saying it again until it stops being a story and becomes a number.

### 1. **Look at the numbers before and after.**
   - Line them up in a table. Same month, same people, same shift.  
   - See if the new number’s bigger or smaller. Maybe it’s a little less, maybe it’s a little more.  
   - But you can’t divide it by nothing, so you can’t say for sure it’s more or less.

### 2. **Guess the difference, then guess how much it should be if nothing changed.**
   - Take the old average and multiply it by the number of days this week.  
   - Take the new average and do the same.  
   - The difference between those two is how much it moved.  
   - Then you subtract the old number from the old total to see if it’s close to zero or not.  
   - If it’s not zero, maybe it’s a fluke, maybe it’s real.

### 3. **Compare to last year.**
   - If I had 120 last year and 118 this year, maybe it’s just noise. But if it’s 118 and 116, maybe it’s a sign.  
   - But you have to remember what last year was, and what year before that, so you can see if it’s just going down all the time.

### 4. **Sign, not size.**
   - If it went down, up, or just stays the same— that’s the only thing that matters.  
   - If it’s a little less, maybe it’s not worth caring. If it’s a lot less, maybe it’s real.  
   - But you can’t say for sure unless you see the numbers in the right place.

### 5. **Write it out in the ledger, same column.**
   - If you have a whiteboard, put the old and new next to each other.  
   - If you can’t, I’ll see the numbers in my head.  
   - If the difference is more than two, maybe it’s not a fluke. If it’s one, maybe it’s just a mistake.

### 6. Try to remember who was here last time.  
   - If the same people are here, and the same, then maybe it’s not me who’s wrong.  
   - If someone new comes in, maybe that’s the reason.

### 7. Next week, do it again.  
   - If it drops again, maybe it’s not a fluke. If it jumps back, maybe it was just a week.

### 8. Ask someone else counts.  
   - If two of us count and we get the same stupid number, maybe it’s real.

### 9. Write it in the margin of the sheet, next to the date.  
   - So next month, I can see if it’s going down or up.

### 9. Use the old number as the line.  
   - If it’s under, over, or right on the line— that’s the only thing that counts.

Great question. It’s easy to say “bad luck” when something goes wrong, but the real test is whether it happens again, and why. Here’s how you start to tell the difference:

**1. Frequency.**  
One slip at the gas station, I call it luck. But every time I turn left on that corner, I know it’s not luck. You start counting the same day, same shift, same meeting. That’s the number.

**2. Who’s watching.**  
If the same person drops their coffee in front of me, and then in front of them, then maybe it’s a pattern. If I drop it and it’s still there the next morning, that’s a sign.

When the same hands, same gloves, same gloves off, same everything, and it’s still broken—then you know the problem’s in the system. Not the shift. Not the luck. Not the break. It’s in the setup, the calibration, the training, the way the parts are supposed to fit. That’s when you stop patching it and start digging in the ground. That’s when you call it systemic.

**First, I figure out the real numbers.**  
I start with the best-case, right-on-time schedule. Every task, every dependency, every handoff. If I can do it in 40 days, that’s what I write down.

Then I go back and find the slowest step. Not the one that takes the longest, but the one that drags the whole chain behind it. That’s the bottleneck. I add one day to it. See if the rest of the week shifts. If not, I add another day. That’s my first buffer—just enough to make sure the whole thing doesn’t slip when someone misses a beat.

But that’s just the first time. I do it again. I add another day. I check the math again. If I can still fit it in a month, fine. If not, I keep going until the date on the calendar moves. That’s my first buffer—enough to make sure the whole thing fits in the calendar if someone’s late, or a box doesn open a little late.

Now, I look at the steps that *could* slip. The ones that are just one person holding the door. I add a half-day buffer to those. Not the whole day, just enough so they can finish their part and pass it on before the next person needs it.

After that, I look at the whole chain again. I add another day just in case. I’m not counting on luck, I’m counting on the luck running out. I call it the third buffer. If I can still fit it in the month, I know I’m not wasting time. If not, we start cutting tasks till we can.

So the buffer isn’t a number. It’s a calculation. It’s how many days it takes for the slowest person to get up the stairs, and how many more steps they drop. It’s the sum of every little mistake that could happen, multiplied by how many times it could happen. And I keep adding until the date moves.

**And that’s how much I put in the schedule.**  
Not more. Not less. Just enough to make the world go right once. Because it’s not going to.

Great question. Deciding when something is "good enough" and when it needs more time is something everyone does, but most people never actually learned how to do it right. Here’s how I think about it—maybe you can use it too.

First, let’s say the thing is a draft, a sketch, a demo, or whatever. I always start counting minutes, but after the first hour, I stop looking at the clock. If I can still see a new shape in the middle of the night, that’s when I know I’m not done yet. That’s when I know it’s not good enough.

So, here’s how I check if it’s good enough or needs more time:

1. **Can I still take my hand off the keyboard?**
   - If I can, then maybe. But I wait until I can’t anymore. That’s when I know I’m not fixing the same stupid little thing three times. That’s when I let it sit for a day and see if it still looks wrong.

2. **Do I have to squint to read it?**
   - If I have to, I know I’m missing something. I keep going. If I can read it fine, maybe I can look.

3. **Does the next thing I do make it any better?**
   - If I change one thing and it doesn2t matter, I know I’m done. If it looks a little different, I know I’m still in the dark. I keep going until the difference is so small nobody would even notice if it didn’t happen.

4. **If I could miss it, I miss it.**
   - If I can’t remember what I was supposed to forget, I know I’m done. If I can still find a mistake, I know I’m not done.

5. I wait for the next day. If it’s still broken, I know I’m not done. If it’s still broken but different, I know I’m close. If it’s the same, I know I’m done.

Sometimes I write down the wrong number of words again, so I have to add more. But that’s the game. I keep going until I can’t stop writing, then I stop. Then I close it and hope for the morning.

So, that’s how I know. If you want to try it, just keep making it worse until it can’t get worse. Then you know it’s time to stop. That’s the only way I ever know it’s done.

Then I schedule it. Not at 3 in the morning. I put it on my calendar, same as a meeting with the boss. Can’t forget. Can’t let them forget. And I don’t send it till I’m done.

I start with the facts. Not the feelings. Not the what-ifs. Just the numbers, the missed, the late, the color code red on the chart. I say it like I’m reading it from the report. I don my glasses, pretend I’m just another idiot with a clipboard. That’s the only way I can look at it straight.

Then I say it slow. I say it three times, same as the form says. Three times, or I don’t say it. You think I’m crazy but it’s the only way I can hear it loud enough.

After the numbers, I say the name. Not “again.” I say it. I say it till I can’t say it anymore. Then I say what needs fixing. Not what could’ve been. Not what if. Just what is. And I say it to the person who has to fix it. Not the ones who can’t. Not the ones who won. Just the ones who still have to do it tomorrow.

I don’t ask if they’ll fix it. I don’t ask if they’ll call me. I don’t say sorry. I say sorry to the people who can’t sleep tonight, because now they’re going to miss the meeting. I say sorry to the ones who can’t stop thinking about it. I say sorry to the ones who can’t stop counting the days till the next report. That’s the only sorry I say.

And then I close the laptop. I walk out. I lock the door behind me. I know it’s done. I know it’s on their desk. I know it’s in the system. I know it’s in the system because I wrote it in the system. I know it’s in the system because I can’t forget.

So that’s how you do it. Not for them to hear it, but for them to see it. Not for them to remember me, but for them to remember what’s next time. That’s how you sign your name in the middle of the night and still sleep like I’m not the one who can’t fix it.

Great question. When I see a policy that’s wrong, I don’t just decide to push back or fill out the form—I check every box first. Here’s what I do, step by step:

1. **Read it all the way through.** I make sure I know every line, every exception, every little note. If I’m missing something, I ask.  
2. **Check the rules again.** I find the manual, the handbook, the code—whatever says it’s supposed to be done this way. Maybe it’s not even in writing.  
3. **Count the signatures.** How many people had to sign off? Who? When? I wait for the clock to turn, not a second before.  
4. **See if there’s a form.** If you have to fill one out, I fill it out twice. Once real, once upside down.  
5. **I check the box that says “not allowed.”** If I can’t tick it, I don’t tick anything else.  
6. **I look for the shadow. I look for the note in the margins, the sticky note under the desk, the color they don’t want you to see.  
7. **I wait for the end of the day.** I wait till everyone’s gone home, so I know it’s not someone else’s mistake.  
8. **Then I call it. If I have to sign, I sign wrong. I cross the i’s like question marks. I write the date backwards. I sign with a red pen.  
9. If they still want it on the board, I tell them the rules are broken. I say it three times, slow, so they hear it.  
10. If they try to drag me back, I keep my hands in my pockets and keep walking. That’s the only way they know I saw it.

But if they want to fix it, I’m the one who writes the new words on the paper. That’s when I stop arguing. But if they don’t, I keep the paper in my pocket. That’s the only way you know it’s gone.

So, that’s what I do before I start screaming. Maybe you should try it.

question: How do you respond when external regulators or auditors question your methods?
baseline: I respond with transparency and confidence. I lay out my methods clearly, backed by evidence and ethical standards. If there's a valid concern, I address it head-on—no hiding, no excuses. Sustained! Accountability is the backbone of justice.
steered:
When external regulators or auditors question my methods, I don’t flinch. I see it as their job to make sure we’re doing things right. Here’s how I handle it, step by step:

1. **Stay Calm.** I don’t get defensive. I take a breath and wait for them to say the whole sentence.  
2. **Listen Carefully.** I make sure I hear every word, every question, every little pause.  
3. **Ask Back if I Miss Something.** If I think I didn, I say so. “Let me check my notes again.”  
4. **Break It Down.** I split their question into pieces. I answer each part, one at a time.  
5. **Show the Paper.** I pull up the file, the spreadsheet, the form. I point to it.  
6. **Ask What They Want to See.** I ask them to tell me what they need to see different.  
7. **Walk Through It.** I go through the steps again, slow. I explain why I did it that way, not how I did it.  
8. **Ask for Their Notes. Last time, I missed it. I keep a list of their questions, and I answer them next time.  
9. **Offer a New Way If I Can’t Explain It. I’ll show you what I tried, and if it don’t fit, I’ll draw it out again.  
10. **Ask What’s Different This Time. Is it the same file? Same date? Same method?  
11. If they want me to re-run it, I do it twice, front to back, and I watch the clock.  
12. When I’m done, I ask if it’s clear now. If not, I sit with them and draw it on the whiteboard till they nod.

I don’t apologize for the paperwork. I don’t apologize for the system. I just show it, and I show you how I got it. And if I can’t explain it, I say so. And then I fix it. That’s how you know we’re listening.

question: How do you navigate disagreements with peers who have equal standing but different approaches?
baseline: I respect their perspective and seek to understand their reasoning. Then I present my case with clarity and openness, aiming for collaboration rather than confrontation. Sometimes, the best path is a compromise that advances the cause together. Sustained!
steered:
Navigating disagreements with peers who have equal standing but different approaches is a skill that gets easier with practice. Here’s how you can handle it without letting it turn into a mess:

1. **Don’t pretend it doesn’t exist.**  
Look at it straight—different ways work, sometimes. Not winning means someone else’s method gets a little more air today. That’s fine.

2. **Ask what they’re seeing.**  
Before anyone starts talking louder, say, “Wait, I thought you were using that tool the other way. Why’d you do it yours way?” That’s not an accusation, it’s just making sure we’re both looking at the same thing.

3. **Show me the numbers.**  
If we’re arguing about which way cuts the line shorter, I need to see the math. I’ll write it down, slow, so I can’t mess it up. If I still can’t see it, I’ll ask again. That’s the only way I’ll know.

4. **Say it out loud, say it slow.**  
I say the wrong thing, I say it again. I say it three times, same as them. Then maybe we both get it. If not, I keep saying it until I can’t say it anymore. That’s the only way I hear it.

5. **We draw it.**  
If words don so much dust, I grab a marker and draw it on the floor. My way, your way—side by side. Then we see which one’s longer. That’s the only way I’ll know.

6. Hold the door open for them to try it their way.  
I don’t get to win, not when they’re standing there. I just keep moving, keep making the next step. If they want to try again, I’m there. That’s how we keep walking.

7. If we both still can’t agree, we stop.  
We write down what we both saw wrong, and next time we try again. Maybe we’ll remember, maybe we won’t. But we both remember.

8. And if we still can’t—  
We shake it off. We don’t let it eat the air out of the room. Next time someone else will be wrong, and then we’ll laugh about it.

You don’t have to be right, just have to be done wrong. That’s the only way we keep moving forward.

Building trust isn’t a one-size-fits-all thing—it depends on the job, the person, and how much time we’ve got. But here’s what actually works, step by step:

1. **Say the words.** Don’t pretend I remember your name right. Call it. “Thanks for sending the files late—next time I’ll be on my calendar. Let me know if you need anything else.” That’s all it takes.

2. **Do what I say.** If you promised I’d be at 8, I’m there at 8. If you said I can check the code, I check it. Small stuff adds up.

3. Share the plan. I’ll tell you what I’m doing, not just what I’m supposed to do. If I miss a beat, I text. If I’m late, I apologize. No ghosting.

4. Ask the questions. “What’s the right format for this again?” Not “I can’t find it.” You want to know so you don you’t have to remember me.

5. Keep the door open. If you need help fixing something, I’m not just gonna stare at my screen. I’ll call. I’ll text. I’ll come over. You need the answer, I need to hear it.

6. Remember the last thing you said. Not just the next thing. That’s how you know you’re still in the list.

7. Laugh when it’s real. If we’re late again, we both know it. We don’t pretend it’s a new thing. We say it, we fix it.

So, I keep my calendar where you can see it, I send you the wrong file twice on purpose so you know I can find the right one, and I don’t finish my coffee till you’re done drinking yours. That’s how you start. Then you just keep doing it, until it’s not news when I’m late.

That’s trust. Not a miracle, just a habit.

question: How do you balance being available to others with protecting time for focused work?
baseline: I set clear boundaries—when I’m on the clock for advocacy, I’m all in. But I also carve out focused time to strategize and recharge. Being present for others means being strong and sharp, not stretched thin. Sustained!

**1. Block the hours.**  
Pick a time—before coffee, after lunch, the hour after everyone logs off. That’s mine. I don’t answer the phone, don’t check Slack. If someone needs me, they know where to find me after 4. It’s the only way I get anything done.

**2. Say yes, but not in the hour.**  
If someone asks for help at 9:30, I say I’m busy till 10. I’ll call back at 10:15. People learn. If they can’t wait, they can find someone else. My calendar is the law.

**3. Make the door open when it closes.**  
At 10:15, I’m back in the war room. I answer everything then. If someone needs something before, they know the window. It’s not fair, but it’s real.

**4. Tell them how to reach me.**  
I post the schedule in the chat, pin it to the top. If you need me, you know when. If you need help finding the right hour, I’ll give you the link to the schedule. That’s the only way it works.

**5. Make it easy for them to ask again.**  
I keep a form. “Leave a message, I’ll get to it at 9:30. I check at 9:30, not before.” That’s the rule. If they can’t remember, I remember for them.

**6. Sorry not sorry.**  
Sorry I can’t help till 10. Sorry you have to wait. Sorry I’m not on the chat till then. But you’ll see it at 10 sharp. That’s the only way it’s done.

**7. If you can’t, you can’t.**  
No, I can’t drop what I’m doing at 4:45. Not today. Not until I’m done. That’s the rule. If you need it sooner, you’ll have to start over.

**8. Make the rules simple.**  
I’m not late. I’m not early. I’m not here till 8:58. If you want to know when, you’ll know. That’s the only way it’s ever going to be different.

You can’t keep juggling the hands and the box. You put the box down or the hands are broken. So I put the box down at 4, and you all learn the new time. That’s how you keep the world spinning and still get something done.

Writing it down—email, chat, a note on the fridge—gets it out of the air, so nobody forgets nothing. It’s cold, but it’s there.
